title: Infra: GPU Fleet, Cloud Networking, IaC Modules, CI/CD & Runbooks (Consolidated)
author: Maya Thompson
content:
Overview

This consolidated playbook documents Redwood's infrastructure engineering guidance for GPU fleet and capacity planning, cloud account and networking patterns, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD and build pipelines, and operational runbooks. It is intended as the single entry point for infra engineers and on-call SREs onboarding to GPU-backed inference services.

Scope
- GPU fleet sizing and autoscaling policies
- Cloud account structure, VPCs, peering, and network security boundaries
- Terraform module conventions and registry usage
- CI/CD pipeline patterns for infra and serving runtime changes
- Runbooks for common incidents and day-2 operations

Ownership and Contacts
- Document owner: infra-platform team (primary: Maya Thompson)
- Supporting teams: eng-serving-runtime, eng-sre, eng-infra-networking
- Pager/On-call: eng-sre primary rota (see /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response)

High-level Architecture (textual)
- Control plane (Redwood control services) in shared infra accounts
- GPU serving fleets in dedicated region-specific accounts with restricted access
- Private deployments (customer VPCs) use cross-account roles and VPC peering or Transit Gateway for connectivity

GPU Fleet & Capacity Planning
- Goals and SLOs:
  - 99th percentile tail latency target: 250ms for short requests (<=256 tokens) on Dedicated capacity
  - Utilization target: 60-70% average GPU utilization for cost efficiency
  - Headroom target: maintain 20% spare capacity for surge buffer during peak traffic
- Capacity types:
  1) Reserved pools (Dedicated) — provisioned, predictable throughput
  2) Preemptible/burst pools — lower-cost, auto-drainable for non-critical workloads
  3) On-demand spillover — cross-region fallback for critical SLA traffic
- Autoscaling policy (recommended):
  - Primary metric: request concurrency per GPU and average free memory percentage
  - Scale up: when 3-minute moving average concurrency per GPU > target_threshold and queue length > 50
  - Scale down: when 15-minute moving average concurrency per GPU < 60% of target and free memory > 40%
- Capacity planning cadence:
  1) Weekly consumption review (owner: infra capacity)
  2) Monthly headroom validation with traffic simulations (owner: eng-sre + product)
  3) Quarterly forecasting aligned with sales reserved capacity commitments

GPU Node Types and Labels
- Node naming: region-pooltype-gpuclass-YYYYMM (e.g. us-west1-dedicated-a100-202611)
- Standard labels/tags:
  - team: infra-platform
  - pool: dedicated|preemptible|burst
  - gpu_class: a100|h100|t4
  - owner: <pager-email>

Cloud Accounts & Networking
- Account topology:
  - org-root: management and billing accounts
  - shared-services account: shared logging, monitoring, IAM automation
  - infra accounts per region: hosting GPU fleets and infra tooling
  - customer-owned accounts for Private deployments: cross-account roles for orchestration
- Networking patterns:
  - VPC-per-account with standardized subnet CIDR allocations (documented in the network CIDR plan)
  - Transit Gateway (or cloud equivalent) for cross-region and cross-account connectivity where low-latency is required
  - VPC endpoints for storage, secrets, and control plane integration to reduce internet egress
- Security controls:
  - Default deny NSGs with explicit allow for control-plane-to-nodes traffic
  - Egress restrictions on GPU fleets to prevent data exfiltration for sensitive workloads
  - Mutual TLS for inter-service RPCs across accounts

Terraform / IaC Modules
- Module registry and conventions:
  - Central module registry located in: git::ssh://git.company/repo/infra-modules (private repo)
  - Naming: module_<purpose> (e.g. module_vpc, module_gpu_node_group, module_iam_cross_account_role)
  - Modules must have: inputs.tf (variables), outputs.tf, examples/, README.md with usage and upgrade notes
- Versioning and releases:
  - Semver for modules (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Breaking changes require a major increment and migration guide
  - All module releases must include changelog and upgrade test plan (example plan: upgrading a staging cluster)
- Example module usage (terraform snippet):
  ```hcl
  module "gpu_node_group" {
    source = "git::ssh://git.company/repo/infra-modules//module_gpu_node_group?ref=v1.4.0"
    region = "us-west1"
    gpu_class = "a100"
    min_size = 2
    max_size = 50
  }
  ```
- Security for IaC:
  - State storage: encrypted remote state (SSE + KMS/HSM) and state locking (DynamoDB / cloud native lock)
  - Secrets: do not store secrets in Terraform variables; use secrets manager references and templates

CI/CD and Build Pipelines
- Pipeline types and responsibilities:
  - infra-ci: validate terraform plan, run static checks, run unit tests for modules (PR gate)
  - infra-deploy: run terraform apply in CI/CD-controlled environment using ephemeral approval for production
  - runtime-build: build and publish serving runtime artifacts (docker images) to internal registry, run image scans
  - canary-deploy: controlled rollout for runtime and infra changes with automatic rollback on key metrics
- Branching and PR requirements:
  - All infra changes require: terraform fmt, terraform validate, full plan on target environment, and 2 approvers (one must be from eng-sre)
  - Protected branches: main and release/* require CI passing and signed commits for releases
- Secrets and credentials in CI:
  - Use federated identity or short-lived service tokens. No long-lived SSH keys in CI.
- Pipeline examples (high level):
  1) PR opened -> run unit tests and tf plan (comment plan on PR)
  2) After approvals -> merge to main triggers infra-deploy to staging
  3) Staging smoke tests -> if green, manual promote to prod with canary policy

Runbooks and Operational Playbooks
- Runbook structure (standard):
  1) Summary and impact
  2) Severity and business impact thresholds
  3) Detection: monitoring alerts and runbook trigger conditions
  4) Immediate mitigation steps (quick actions to restore service)
  5) Diagnostics (log queries, metrics to inspect)
  6) Root cause fixes and long-term remediation
  7) Post-incident actions and owners

- GPU OOM / Node memory pressure
  1) Summary: nodes running out of GPU memory causing inference OOMs or process crashes
  2) Detect: increased OOM metrics, coredumps, elevated 5xx errors, alert: gpu_memory_oom_rate > 0.5%/5m
  3) Mitigation steps:
     a) Temporarily redirect traffic to alternative pool (runbook command: rctl route set --route inference --pool preemptible-burst)
     b) Scale up node group: terraform apply or autoscaler override (CLI example: gcloud compute instance-groups managed resize ...)
     c) Restart failing pods/containers gracefully (kubectl rollout restart deployment/serving-runtime)
  4) Diagnostics commands:
     - kubectl describe node <node-name>
     - nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total --format=csv
     - check runtime logs: journalctl -u serving-runtime.service --since "10m"
  5) Post-incident: increase memory threshold alerts, add pre-warming for model caches

- Node termination / Preemptible eviction
  1) Summary: preemptible nodes evicted, causing capacity loss and request latency spikes
  2) Mitigation: drain and cordon new nodes, spin up replacement nodes in non-preemptible pool, enable spillover to other region per policy
  3) Preventative controls: maintain <10% critical traffic on preemptibles, prefer pre-warmed caches on dedicated pools

- CI/CD Failure during prod deploy
  1) Summary: terraform apply or image promotion fails mid-deploy
  2) Immediate actions: stop pipeline, notify on-call, evaluate terraform plan state and lock status
  3) Recovery: if partial apply, use state inspection and roll back by applying last-known-good plan or restoring state snapshot

Observability and Alerting (short guide)
- Key metrics to monitor:
  - per-GPU throughput (tokens/s), avg latency, p95/p99 latency, GPU utilization, GPU memory used
  - infra health: node restart rate, image pull failures, terraform apply failures rate
- Alerting thresholds (examples):
  - p99 latency > 2x baseline for 5 minutes -> P1 incident
  - GPU utilization > 90% sustained for 10 minutes -> paging alert for capacity follow-up (not page for short bursts)
  - autoscaler error rate > 1% -> investigate autoscaling infra

Operational Playbook: Major Release (infra or runtime)
1) Prepare: update module versions, run full tf plan in staging, run integration tests against staging fleet
2) Canary: deploy to 5% of capacity or a dedicated canary pool, monitor telemetry for 30 minutes
3) Promote: if canary stable, promote in waves (25% -> 50% -> 100%) with 10-minute observation windows
4) Rollback: if metrics breach thresholds, automatically rollback to previous artifact via CI-CD rollback step and scale down faulty nodes

Compliance and Audit Notes
- All module changes and production infra changes must be tracked in git with signed commits and link to change ticket (JIRA id)
- Terraform state and plan artifacts are retained for 90 days for audit, with access logged via centralized logging account

Appendices
- Useful CLI snippets:
  - Terraform plan for account X: TF_VAR_account_id=123 terraform plan -var-file=env/staging.tfvars
  - Force a node group resize: ./scripts/resize-node-group --region us-west1 --group us-west1-dedicated-a100 --count 10
  - Fetch recent OOM logs: aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name /serving-runtime --start-time $(date -d '10 minutes ago' +%s000)

- Reference documents:
  - infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026 (detailed module docs)
  - gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026 (full runbook collection)
  - infra-gpu-ci-cd-iac-guidelines-2026 (CI/CD specific rules)

Maintenance and Review Cadence
- This document owner will review quarterly and after any P1 incident affecting GPU capacity or cross-account networking. Major changes to IaC modules or account topology require an ADR and a rolling review with eng-sre and security teams.

End of document.
